comments.name: quentin c.
comments.body:
"The president, who isn’t known for his embrace of new ideas, might see anti-communism as an easy path to victory.
***
The president himself gestures toward this game of copycat when he hails Andrew Jackson or praises William McKinley as a man who made America great." 

Exactamundo. He's been doing this since at least 2016, when his campaign was pretty much a pastiche of successful slogans from more recent campaigns than Andy Jackson and McKinley (perhaps he now wants to align himself with the Supreme Court conservatives' touting of "history and tradition). In 2016, he lifted "Make America Great Again" from Reagan (a phrase also used by Bill Clinton), and he's currently trying to outdo Reagan's Star Wars boondoggle with his proposed Golden Dome. He took his appeal to blue collars from Nixon's courting of hardhats and Clinton's outreach to the forgotten middle class . His xenophobia echoes Pat Buchanan. He glommed on to Obama's successful use of data analytics and social media.

He's not original, but he's pretty astute judge of what has worked before. Let's hope the "communist!" label is too ancient to be retrieved from the dustbin of history.

comments.body:
The irony is that no president in American history has posed more of a threat to the free market than Donald Trump. He's weaponized federal agencies so that he can personally choose winners and losers--among law firms. broadcast stations, billionaires vying for multi-billion dollar NASA contracts, and every business. Trump believes that he can buy golden shares of a business and make corporate decisions, like whether a CEO should be fired or where a business should expand. He uses tariffs as a weapon to exact concessions from CEOs. He does the same thing when extracting concessions from countries. He believes himself to have as much control over the economy as any emperor.

Rightwing media are usually careful to call the opposition Marxism or Boshevism in order to imply that what these Democratic Socialist candidates favor is old-fashioned twentieth century authoritarianism. Those are words that older Americans fear, although I don't think they resonate as much with younger voters. Of course, these candidates are all anti-authoritarian and anti-communist. Ironically, most Americans would agree with their actuaol policy positions.

comments.name: Dave
comments.body:
Once again, a case of Trump simply amplifying what hate radio has been fomenting and "test driving" for years - which is virulently castigating anyone who isn't 100% on the Trump Train as being incontrovertibly and diabolically "communist".

The entire far-right media ecosystem has been seeding the ground with the "communist" bogeyman ever since Trump lost the 2020 election. Biden was a "communist". The mainstream media is run by "communists". The entire American educational system (from K thru PhD) has been totally infiltrated by "communists". All of Europe (except for the now-deposed Viktor Orban) is "communist".

This has been Trump's bottom line, go-to demonization strategy ever since he started campaigning for his second term back in early 2024. All of his blatantly neo-fascist rallies that year included his bellowing, theatrical condemnations of "the radical left lunatics" and the "Marxists, communists and fascists" who "hate our country" - and thus represent the dreaded "Enemy Within".

Sure, it's nothing more than warmed-over, mutilated McCarthyism - repurposed for a generation of Americans who have no memory of what a foul, despicable, hate-filled excuse for a human being that Sen. Joe McCarthy was before he drank himself to death.

But it's working. Which says far more about the abysmal state of American education and civic virtue in general than it does about the psychopathic demagogue who now wields McCarthy's tired, hateful rhetoric as if it were something new.

For the very rich, though,  regulation is a constant threat to further enrichment and socialism or communism a far worse threat to their massive wealth than the mere loss of any number of human lives.

comments.body: Two pieces of advice for today's grads: Try not to get involved AT ALL in office politics, and understand that being friendly with the boss doesn't guarantee anything, including job security. Build a life away from your work.

comments.name: Martin
comments.body:
These types of articles make me wonder about many things.  My opinion is based on my niece who works about 2 hours a day as naturopath, now travels the world with her baby and boyfriend, who works about 4 months out of the year in construction.  Because of world travel he is basically part time worker, and they both complain they will never be able to afford a house in this economy.  They even complain that her boyfriend's employer refuses to hold jobs for him when he's returned from travel and announces his re-availability.  

They sacrifice nothing for their goal of owning a home.  

Yes, things are more expensive but I too can harp on the days when a slice of pizza cost $1, or something else ridiculous like that.  I planned, worked, and sacrificed many things through economic upheavals and large price increases to own my home.  Why this fact is so cavalierly discounted by so many people is beyond me.  My house wasn't handed to me by some magical economy.  It took years and years of work and planning.

So, perhaps for some the economy is part of the problem ( I do think we have some major problems with wealth distribution), but for many people complaining, the economy doesn't tell the entire story.  Far from it.

comments.name: @drakebaer
comments.body: This Gen Z take on work is so old-fashioned! “Tune in, turn on, drop out” was the mantra of under-30s in the 1960s. My “slacker generation” born then was oriented to slough off work, according to generalizing pundits. My parents were born in the mid-1930s. They and their cohorts had professions but defined themselves counter-culturally, through open-marriage, women’s liberation and loud protests of the status quo, especially corporate values. This wasn’t a small minority of Americans; just look at the highest grossing books of the late ‘60s through late ‘70s. Yes, the corporate ethic of college-educated Americans defining themselves through work seems a value of many millennials and their late-boomer parents. But I’d argue the rest of us born since WWII have been more closely aligned with Gen-Z in our attitudes towards work, while in our 20s, than with millennials and late-boomers.

comments.name: Jeff
comments.body: Well researched and written. Kudos. At 22 I believed that regardless of education and family that if I worked harder and learned more about my vocation every day that I would succeed and meet my goals. There were ups and there were downs (most of them self inflicted) but the overall trajectory was up in knowledge, up in career $$ and career enjoyment. I never stopped pressing to learn more, be more and in later years - save more. Mission accomplished. Now I am retired, comfortable and happy beyond my dreams. I don’t believe that it’s not possible anymore. In 70 years I experienced lots of economic upheaval, high unemployment, much higher interest rates than today and political messes. As I look around my area there are multi million dollar houses and also two to three hundred thousand dollar houses. Who starts with the house of their dreams? Maybe I am just a geezer but I see plenty of opportunities for college or high school graduates, just not instant riches and country clubs except for the fortunate few - as always. I kept my nose to the grindstone for 50 years and it paid off. I understand that is not for everyone, however, I feel that if you are not willing to do the work- quit whining about the economy. It’s not the economy- it’s you.

comments.name: VPW
comments.body: I’m a retired boomer and always felt there was something out there for me.  I had a 35 year career in accounting at a few different employers but for the most part I felt motivated and engaged and was paid enough to have a wife who could work part time and raise our children.   We did live modestly but certainly not poor.  I feel fortunate. I do feel for the students coming out now.  The world is changing before our eyes and the workforce will look significantly different in rapid fashion.   It must be a scary outlook but I agree with those who say it’s important to keep looking forward.  It’s the only way to find your “way”

comments.name: liz
comments.body:
Hey, I don't deny that times are really, really hard for today's young people, and who are looking for jobs.  I also completely agree that a 'career'...climbing the corporate ladder... making bucketloads of money and having the trappings of 'success', ain't all it's cracked up to be.

And when it comes to lower-tier workers, most salaries are not sufficient on which to live from.

At the same time, however, I've really disliked the social-media driven mentality that all or most employers are 'evil'.... that employers have a 'lot of nerve' to want workers to come into the office, etc.  Some people have swung too far the other way in this respect.  

Working for an employer is a two-way street.  You are performing a service for them, and in return, they provide you with a salary (and varying levels of benefits).  When you were hired, you agreed to the particular terms of the job.  So for some folks to then suggest that such employer expectations is unreasonable, is childish and naive, to say the last.  That's not employers being 'abusive'.  That's simply how work, works.

comments.name: L
comments.body:
I am a millennial software engineer and a homeowner, but I don't believe in the inherent goodness of work. The output of work can be beneficial, and contributing to society can be a net good, but far too many people are alienated from the fruits of our labor. To somewhat mangle Marx, we don't make a complete shoe, but merely glue the sole on over and over. Instead of building technologies to improve the world, they are being bent to shape maximum engagement, maximum ad dollars, maximum extraction from the worker drones, detrimental knock on effects  contributing to the breakdown of society notwithstanding.

Worker productivity has dramatically outpaced wages. The spoils go increasingly to those wealthy enough to have their income tied primarily to the casino shaped stock market. The social contract is gone - hard work won't save you when your insanely profitable employer doesn't grow as quickly as hoped and the layoffs come. We only have one life to live, and the corporate oligarchs aren't worth dying for, much less living for.

I’ve delayed a lot of gratification but never to the point of feeling completely deprived. The secret is to be content with less. I retired two months ago and am greatly enjoying the luxury of time and freedom I have now.

comments.name: Aram Hollman

Dear American,

In my wisdom, I've decided that there's no point taxing billionaires on their income (or their dividends, or their interest). Instead, I'm going to tax you, not directly but indirectly. When you buy something imported, you'll pay part (most) of the tariff on it. Since we want this to create American jobs, tariffs will allow American producers to charge more for the same item. You'll pay that too.

You'll pay enough in additional tariffs to make the One Big Beautiful Bill sufficiently revenue-neutral. In short, you'll pay the cost of the additional tax cuts for rich people that are built into to the OBBB.

And remember, you benefit from this too. If you're a 70-year-old for whom Social Security isn't enough to live on, such that you've gone back to work part-time as a bagger in the local grocery store, remember, I'm not taxing your Social Security benefits either. So don't be too resentful of the millions in tax cuts that Bezos, Zuckerberg, and others will get, because you're getting yours, too.

Thank you for your attention to this matter.

DJT

comments.name: Statute of Liberty
comments.body:
While I think everything about Trump’s economic policies are stupid and petty, people in this country really need to think long and hard about where the things they buy are made. 
The United States is going to be a failed state if we don’t get back to manufacturing things here. 
The (next) government really needs to get serious about passing laws and creating regulations that reign in private equity. For two long these entities have been allowed unfettered to not, as the monitor “private equity” connotes, inject private funds into companies, but rather gut them and sell whatever parts remain to Chinese interests.
Congress also needs to pass the Country of Origin Online Labeling Act. It is beyond ridiculous that online sellers are not required to state where the products they are selling have been made. The old excuse that it takes too long to provide that information just doesn’t cut it anymore given all of the technological advances.
It also is incumbent on Americans to care where the products they buy were made. That means not complaining about the loss of decent-paying jobs in this country at the same time as you are filling up your cart at some big-box store with products made in China or some other country with cheap labor and poor working conditions.

As we all know, the tariffs are a tax on the American people.  And they increase the rate of inflation that we all are paying.  One big issue not talked about is who the tariffs affect most. comments.name: David Flannery
comments.body:
While true that the DSA is gaining influence in the Democratic Party, they ain't yet in a position to control the party.  Remember, they have less than 10 believers in the current Congress.  That said, there is nothing but good sense in Mr. Rove's words that:  "Today, if you don’t like a job, grocery store, restaurant, doctor, hospital, car or airline, you can pick another. Because free markets empower you as a consumer, you have technology, services and goods that in the past would have been available only to the very wealthy, if at all."

Socialism is not the answer to the economic challenges we face.  But neither is continuing policies that promote the lopsided wealth and income disparities that exist.

The DSA appeals far more strongly to young people who can't see a way to make the American Dream come true even when they attend or finish college.  The optics of a president earning over $2 billion last year is, to say the least, unhelpful.  

Tax cuts won't float the boats stranded on the beaches.  Give-a-ways won't encourage people to work harder.  Compromise over new concepts and policies are necessary.  

One thing that Rove gets wrong is health care.  He writes: “Universal healthcare at no cost to individuals” is one of many “free” things government will dispense."  There is no such thing as a free lunch but there are better ways to fund the health care needs of our citizens.  In my view, a single-payer system (Meidcare for all) may work better than the current system.

That right wing sub-controversy made it a treat to read an article in this newspaper earlier this week, headlined 'Here’s What Greeks Think of Nolan’s ‘The Odyssey.’ (It’s Their Story, After All.)'

Reporter Niki Kitsantonis described the reactions of the actual Greeks who have seen and commented on the film, which has provoked mixed reactions and a variety of critical assessments in Greece as elsewhere.

The the overall response appears to have been largely positive. A few angry far right Greek nationalists have attacked the film on the usual grounds of wokeness, and some viewers and reviewers have sniffed it was too "Hollywood," but on the whole audiences have responded with appreciation.

The Odyssey has long inspired artists to take their own shot at reworking the epic. From James Joyce (Greek scholars emphatically praised his Ulysses) to the Coen Brothers (Greek audiences loved O Brother, Where Art Thou?), it has been worked and reworked again and again. It never gets old.

He was brought up to be totally responsible for his own life by the men and women in the family who raised him - nothing is beneath him - cooking, cleaning, taking care of household and family things.  I am so fortunate. 
The other day we had a power outage and I went to call the electric company and he said "what's the rush, why are you getting all excited - I'm sure the neighbors will call" (we live in an HOA/connected townhomes community). It turned out that we were the only ones affected, due to our own tenant circuit breaker going bad - if we had waited, nothing would have been done by our neighbors. 
When we went to inspect the breaker outside, I said, "the power company told me we need to reset it ourselves - and why don't we open that black tab near our electric meter, since there doesn't seems to be any other visible circuit breakers in the utility closet?"  No, he tells me, that can't be it. So we called the company to send a technician out.  It turns out the circuit breaker was under that tab. 
That day, I wondered what brought on his responses to me.  I'm guessing it was that I "took his agency" as a man to respond first to a small emergency....but to me, I was just doing my part.  Lesson learned; it seems there is an inborn programming of that in men....and I don't mind recognizing and trying to work with that...it seems to be their nature:)

There is a hereditary condition called “short sleeper syndrome” where folks seem to function just fine, with no ill effects, on 4 hours or so of sleep. It’s rare, affecting maybe 2% of the population.  

I definitely do NOT have this syndrome ( I feel best on a solid 8 hours - and enjoy sleeping that long) but perhaps the Japanese Prime Minister has this particular blessing/curse syndrome.

comments.name: J M W
comments.body: What I enjoyed about this article is the fact that the writer did not ask whether her husband was in the background supporting her or whether he was also overworked taking care of their children. In fact, the writer presumes the irrelevancy of such support or lack thereof and does not even mention her marital status. Bravo! This is astute, non-sexist reporting!

comments.name: Randy
comments.body: Don't forget that Takaichi is, and always has been, extremely conservative. She was totally opposed to allowing women to ascend to the Imperial throne, and holds very traditional views on most social issues (married couples should not be allowed separate surnames; same-sex marriages should not be recognized, etc.) That is where you get her silly, theatrical comments about staying up all night ironing underwear and handkerchiefs and sewing on buttons. She earns a significant salary and if she doesn't already have household staff to take care of such things (assuming they even need to be done) she could easily hire them. Of course, they'd better be Japanese nationals, or Sanseito will raise a ruckus.

comments.name: KS
comments.body: In Japan, the word “karoshi” was sometimes used as the cause of death.  It means death from overwork.  I spent a bit of time in Japan and recall an initiative to end karoshi, but it seems the PM has not gotten on board.

comments.name: Steven B.
comments.body:
Both Trump and PM Takaichi are birds of a feather - night owls.
Definitely not healthy.
Whilst she works her clackers off, Trump pumps out garbage all night - but does not get up till late.
I hope people around her can persuade her that sleep deprivation is bad news - I can testify to that.

comments.name: Frglpe
comments.body: No hero to me. Regardless -male or female , it’s not healthy to go without sleep.

comments.name: D
comments.body: I’ve worked in Japan for over a decade and very closely with govt. officials. Working hours are stupidly grueling with next-day deadlines often arriving in inboxes at 6 or 7 p.m. But despite all that rushing and pushing, projects pile up and move like molasses through layers of bureaucracy. Takaichi is promoting performative burnout, not govt. efficiency or progress.

comments.name: Andrea
comments.body: For Pete’s sake, can’t she pay somebody to do her ironing?!

articles.title: Japan Is Startled by Prime Minister’s Grueling Sleep Schedule
articles.byline: Javier C. Hernández and Hisako Ueno
articles.summary: Sanae Takaichi has said she gets just “zero to three hours” of sleep a night, prompting a debate in the country over work-life balance.

comments.name: Al
comments.body: I know it'll never happen, but I'd sure like a line-by-line budget for that $95B.  That's ninety five thoujsand million dollars, a small fraction of what "defense" wants mext year.  What are we getting for all this torrent of cash?

comments.name: Keith wheelock
comments.body:
As a 92 year old who served in federal government under four presidents, I am astonished how the Trump administration is handling its February 28th ‘military excursion’ in Iran.

So far this Trump folly has triggered a global energy crisis, the loss of thousands of Iranian lives, and a few American dead and wounded. The prospect for great American losses is high.

How can the House (and Senate) simply ignore that this foolish war has not been seriously discussed in Congress, much less sanctioned, and is already costing us about $100 billion in military costs?

The effort to include Iranian military costs, a subsidy to affected, and an unconstitutional SAVE bill I find an absurdity that will stall in the Senate.

I wonder what Trumpublicans in the House are thinking, since their stance is overwhelmingly rejected in public polls.

comments.name: David
comments.body: Mr. Arrington: please define “finish the job.” We are six months in and do not have a clear mission or success condition in Iran. The lack of an expectation that the administration provide the reason we are spending American blood and treasure is simply astounding.

comments.name: Betsy Handler
comments.body: Where are the young folks who should be marching against this war? I’m 82, but was a (small) part of the anti-Vietnam War at the University of Wisconsin. Don’t they know? Don’t they care?

comments.name: BjornFree
comments.body: If reconciliation was a maneuver created to make it easier to pass bills that reduce federal deficits then how does this qualify?  Our system is completely broken.

comments.name: Jonathan
comments.body:
The war is a hot mess and Mr. Trump is just winging it each day, with predictably disastrous results, and lying about it constantly. He should be called on the carpet about it. Instead the Republicans in Congress are fanning the flames of the illusion that the situation is in hand. Anyone who reads this (or any legitimate and comprehensive) newspaper knows that we are in a deep strategic and diplomatic hole that Mr. Trump himself dug.

Yes the war is far away. Yes $4 gas isn't the end of the world. Yes "ending Iran's nukes" and "defanging Iran's regime" are feel-good concepts. But servicemembers have been killed. For nothing. We've achieved nothing and we're on track to achieve nothing. For God's sake, MAGA, wake up. Somebody, wake them up. Your Republican legislators are easing your way to catastrophic failure.

comments.name: Nahpets
comments.body: The thing reeks of bad government. How does piling another $73 billion onto the burning pyre of Pentagon funding qualify for "deficit reducing" legislation? Tack on $12 billion to bail out farmers to compensate for the damage that Trump's tariffs have done, and $10 billion for voter suppression, and we have the mother of all bad legislation. The Republican Party is driving our economy and our society off a cliff if they manage to push this through. The party of "fiscal responsibility and family values" What a laugh.

comments.name: Jon
comments.body: They always forget that its our tax money that they are spending.

articles.title: House Adopts $95 Billion G.O.P. Budget for Iran War
articles.summary: Republican leaders muscled through resistance in their own ranks to approve the budget blueprint for the war and other measures, but its prospects were far dimmer in the Senate.

comments.name: K Quaintance
comments.body: How do you make arrangements to visit?

comments.name: RAnnBrunIsDumb
comments.body: A great news story on days when we are short these fascinating, epic accomplishments.

comments.name: Rachel K
comments.body: Thank you for this fascinating article. My friend and I have been wanting to visit Star Axis for years. I can’t believe it’s finally finished. Nearby in Montezuma is the Light Sanctuary, a wonderful installation that is free to visit. Charles Ross designed the prisms that refract sunlight into ever-changing bands of color throughout the year. You can almost feel the rotation of the earth when sitting there. Worth a visit.

comments.name: R. M.
comments.body: Awesome!!!

comments.name: kathy
comments.body: Just amazing. Incredible that someone can even think up this monument that is like following a star up a staircase.

comments.name: Laura
comments.body: Absolutely stunning! Evocative of the pyramids.

comments.name: Jabbey
comments.body: Flies in the face of Leave No Trace. The mesa didn't need art to see the stars.

comments.name: Ryan
comments.body: I would imagine trying to actually see this would involve long lines, irritating tourists, a smartphone app of some sort. And it’s kind of ugly!! Sorry. It must be nice to be super rich though.

articles.title: He’s the Last Great Land Artist You’ve Never Heard Of
articles.summary: Charles Ross spent 50 years building “Star Axis,” a naked-eye observatory in New Mexico. Now his masterwork is ready. How to share it with a changed world?

articles.title: Rwanda, Israel and the Inversion of ‘Genocide’
articles.summary: When Hamas defenders accuse the Jewish state, they follow a trail the Hutus blazed in 1993.

comments.name: Elsie Angeline
comments.body:
Boko Haram, a violent extremist terrorist organization responsible for mass killings and human rights atrocities — has slaughtered more than 100,000 Christians, including women and children, and it barely registers in the news. 

Their goal is openly genocidal. There was no single-day massacre like Israel faced on 10/7 — just relentless, ongoing ethnic cleansing.

And unlike Israel, Boko Haram doesn’t offer ceasefires, negotiations, or conditions. They don’t say “surrender and we’ll stop.” They simply continue wiping out Christian communities.

Yet you won’t see college campuses shut down over it. You won’t see activists flooding the streets. You won’t see the same people who rage online suddenly discovering their moral outrage. Why? 

Because as monstrous as Boko Haram is, they are not Jewish — and that’s the one group certain activists reliably target.. The selective outrage speaks for itself.

comments.name: Charles Vermont
comments.body: Israel has and is fighting a war of self-defense. It's only propaganda from what I refer to as the jabaabadaba nightmare world that pursues the charge of genocide and also idiots on the Left.

comments.name: jeffrey klein
comments.body:
"genocide"????

112,00 trucks with over two million tons of food, 9,600 tons of medical items, and other supplies came through Israel into Gaza during the war.

Israel transferred a million doses of polio vaccine into Gaza, enough to inoculate the entire population under 18.

Every day seven liters of Israeli desalinated water for every man, woman, and child come into Gaza through Israeli pipelines.

There has never been a genocide in world history where the victim population has actually INCREASED.  

"Genocide" poppycock.

comments.name: Peter Aitken
comments.body: Those accusing Israel of genocide are not "Hamas supporters" with maybe a few exceptions. They are serious, respected organizations horrified by Hamas's actions but unwilling to turn a blind eye to Israel's response. They include organizations of Jews, some in Israel.

comments.name: C Thurman
comments.body:
A partial list of organizations that assert that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza: UN high commissioner on Human Rights, the International Association of Genocide Scholars, Amnesty International, Doctors Without Borders, B'Tselem, Physicians for Human Rights–Israel, International Federation for Human Rights, Human Rights Watch.

Among mid-east scholars polled, about 80-90% believe Israel committed genocide or war crimes akin to it in Gaza.

This doesnt change the fact that Hamas also committed genocide on 10/7. Nor that Israel is colonizing the West Bank.

Fun Q to ask: what makes the article author worthy of this esteemed page? Is it part of his doctoral thesis? Or maybe the Rupertbots are willing to condescend to any mouthpiece to issue their propaganda....

comments.name: jeffrey klein
comments.body:
"There will only be peace when Arabs love their own children more than they hate us."

Golda Meir

comments.name: E Stewart S
comments.body: I read Omar Bartov's book  "Israel, What Went Wrong", and it is a much more nuanced and detailed discussion of the issue of genocide, and Israel's possible engagement in it.   Bartov is a renown expert on the issue and definition of genocide. which has been debated for decades.   As Bartov  discusses, he originally did not believe that Israel committed genocide, but changed his position as the Gaza war contuned.  In addition, Bartov actually served in the Israeli military and is familiar with its military's  self imposed operational parameters which he argues have been breached.   I would suggest the those interested  in a more in depth review of this subject read his book.

comments.name: Alon ZoG
comments.body:
Fascinating is that since the year 70 Europeans and Arabs have taken turns expelling and exterminating Jews from the Holy Land and their own countries.  

Christianity and Islam both branched off from Judaism.  Yet, members from both sides deny Jewish connection to the land and pretend the 20th Century ethnic cleansing of Jews from the Arab world didn’t happen.  

And liberals here fully endorse the intolerance of Jews that brought us to where we are today.  Accusations of Israel’s genocide erupted on October 8th.  Clearly the only genocidal intent—against Israeli and Gazans—came from Hamas.

comments.name: Beth
comments.body: Right on for the response to the two mom parents. When you form a family in an unconventional way you are going to get questions. Gentle, child affirming responses are needed. Little ears are listening. How do I know? We adopted from China and we aren’t Asian. It’s not fair to foist the awkwardness on a child- which is what you do when you don’t address this stuff adroitly.

comments.name: mzwong
comments.body: In my server experience, the diners who ask your name and want introductions around the table are the diners who will happily shout for you across the restaurant when they need a water refill, have a question, etc - not paying attention to the fact that you are currently engaged helping other diners. These are also the diners who will leave the smallest tip, having taken up the most time. Yes, being a server means being friendly and efficient, and that can be done without giving out your name to every table. The faux-relationship of this and the expectation that your server will be a part of your entertainment day after day, table after table, can be exhausting. My two cents.

comments.name: Bewildered
comments.body: re: Queer parents.  The problem is not the friendly people who are making an effort to connect, but your aversion to their good intentions.  No, not every woman is "mom:" as other comments point out, children often choose their own designations for caregivers.  Do you judge them too?  And yes, some donors are welcomed as "Dad."  If you are going to set rules about how people (including children) refer to you, you're going to have to put some extra effort into instructing them.

comments.name: A person
comments.body:
When I was pregnant with my first, a coworker of my husband's (who I knew as a social acquaintance) started to call with increasing frequency as I neared our due date. Once, she asked me how much I was dilated or effaced. (If you don't know, she was asking about my cervix.) I replied, "The doctor says everything looks great." She tried to ask again in another way. I said I had to go and hung up. 

LW1 I was expecting questions like THAT. What a letdown to find out you're offended by being asked what your kids would call you! I was asked that too - Mommy, mama, mom, ma - those are all options where I live. People are usually just trying to make conversation, and you have to admit it's more appropriate than asking about someone's cervix.

comments.name: Dan
comments.body:
Although there is indeed no burden of responsibility to educate others about one's family life ... these "clueless" questions or comments nevertheless offer opportunities for appropriate replies (that are not "comebacks" or "zingers").

It would be helpful if some such useful replies were suggested.

comments.name: mo
comments.body:
Two thoughts: 
When I was a server I didn't like it when customers used my name. It felt way too familiar. 
I understand why the couple in the first letter make a distinction between "donor" and "dad". 
But in reality, the donor IS the father, or dad, of the child. It's just that the adults involved have decided that the child is not going to have a relstionship with their father.  Which I personally find really sad. I think it's a heck of a thing to lose.

comments.name: Golf Widow
comments.body:
I'll admit, after seeing the headline I was hoping to read some truly outrageous questions and comments and share the LW's contempt for all those numbskulls. I love juicy, scandalous, "did she really say that?" columns. Alas. 

Unfortunately, the examples LW offered were not even close to being offensive. Being put out by the question about what the baby will call you? Buckle up, buttercup. If that bothers you, you're going to have to recalibrate. Parenting is a rough ride. Best to approach others with openness and kindness and build a strong community. 

If you're lucky and haven't alienated all your acquaintances, perhaps someone will become the kind of good friend with whom you can chuckle about how horrified you were that time she asked what your and your partner's mom names would be. And how you thought, "both mom, DUH?" And how silly that was.... 

Sheesh.

comments.name: Yavnu
comments.body: As a queer grandma, it was a special task to come up with grandma names for the seven grandmothers of our first grandchild (and yes, there were stupid questions -- we just shined them on).    I chose to be Nana T, which my son in law turned into Nanatee the Manatee.  Now that there are more grandkids, I love being Nanatee to all.

articles.title: Should Queer Parents Have Zingers Ready for Boneheaded Questions?
articles.summary: Two moms who are tired of intrusive comments about sperm donation and “mom names” want quippy comebacks they can roll out as needed. Is there a better way?

comments.name: Chris Petruzzi
comments.body:
As a former hedge fund manager and an investor in non-performing mortgages, I am skeptical about Donald Trump's claims to have been "very, very rich" before he was elected in 2016.      After he defaulted on loans in the 1990's US financial institutions would not lend to him.    Then, Deustche Bank lent him money in the middle of the financial crisis on dubious credit statements .    Word Finance reported "Germany’s largest lender, Deutsche Bank, reportedly approved substantial loans to Donald Trump prior to his presidency, during a time he was considered ‘untouchable’ by other Wall Street banks" and wrote that there were "multiple red flags" in the loans.

        I suspect that an anonymous investor  provided cash or other security for his loans.     Since become POTUS Trump has been building his net worth which might otherwise have been zero.

comments.name: Bill Connor
comments.body:
Clearly this is Hunter Biden's Laptops fault...

I really wonder if there is a "bottom" where MAGA will say "whoa, thats corrupt AF Donnie"?

I am not holding my breath. 

For the record, Trump's teleprompter technican grifted more from the US Presidency than Obama, Clinton or Biden and it is a rounding error in the billions of grift that Trump has claimed in just the past year.

comments.name: Mike T
comments.body: The least surprising development imaginable at this point. If there is another way to monetize the office of the presidency, we'll see it as soon as they think of it. The war has ended and restarted a dozen times, each bringing the opportunity of Trump friends and benefactors to make money. Rince and repeat ad nauseum ....

comments.name: Ryan S
comments.body: Where do we go from here?  Our country is being sold to the highest bidder, and we are completely distracted by culture wars.

comments.name: Ryan Tryzbiak
comments.body:
This is blatantly self-dealing but the political and media establishment has long decided that Trump's self-dealing and usage of the office to line his own personal pockets is perfectly acceptable.

In any other era, the president selling inside information for the purpose of gaining an advantage over competing traders, would have, once discovered, been a massive scandal that would ignite a political firestorm and lead to the swift end of that president's tenure.  Now, it's not even the top story in WSJ's daily email digest.

comments.name: Paul C
comments.body: Remember all of those folks with so-called "Trump derangement syndrome" who warned that Trump 2.0 would be all the more dangerous because he'd be totally uninhibited by at least a few reasonable and competent advisers and the remaining constraints imposed on his power by the Constitution? Trump is openly monetizing the fact of his market-moving social media pronouncements and there is nothing we can do, even though everyone knows it's grotesque. SCOTUS has him covered with immunity and the Department of Justice hasn't one shred of independence.

comments.name: Dennis Grossman
comments.body: Clearly illegal.  What a disgrace.

comments.name: Stephen Marshall
comments.body: How can this be legal?

comments.name: Joell
comments.body:
Back when I could watch the TV channel Russia-Today on my Bell Network, I could compare their coverage with that of CBC and Global, such as when a Russian foreign minister spoke at a European meeting, begging that Ukraine be left neutral. None of what he said would be reported on the western mainstream news. Nor did they report that there was a violent coup that overthrew the government of Ukraine in 2014, bringing in extreme ethnic nationalists with a sprinkling of Neo-Nazis--whose first move was to ban the Russian language. There were two attempts at peace agreements that were sabotaged. Only after years of attacks against them, did the ethnic Russians of the east ask for Russia's protection. That's just a short summary of the reasons for the war. Now, readers can go to RT.COM for the Russia media.

Ms. Joell Vanderwagen
journey_publications@sympatico.ca

comments.name: Natalia Kuzmyn
comments.body:
Such a conflicted report, but heavily slanted towards Putin's side of the board. To say that Putin knows the war's results will determine Russia's global reputation is tantamount to suggesting that if Russia is victorious, it will either regain its reputation for military dominance or it will be respected for winning. Yet neither scenario is remotely possible. Not because they're entirely unlikely to win; a desperate Putin may order nuclear bombing, but that would be short-lived glory immediately upon the West's promised response. Because it's clear that Ukrainians are better at this than they are, and because Russia's entire unjustified endeavour has been executed over long years of unspeakable war crimes, their global standing cannot hope to improve for generations to come. 

Russia's endurance rests entirely with what little treasury can still be thrown at a draining cause, and, moreover, depends on the resolve and strengthening resistance of Ukraine and her allies. Endurance, in Putin's failing economy, can indeed surrender to more pressing demands.

comments.name: Wim Roffel
comments.body:
The article illustrates the blindness of many Americans for how their look on the rest of the world is distorted by propaganda by the US government. The article contains many inconsistencies that any Russian diplomat will be happy to point out:
 - Russia invaded Ukraine because it didn't want it to join NATO. Russia can point to many occasions where the US promised not to expand NATO. It can also point to the Cuba crisis as precedent.
 - The goal of the invasion was not a land grab but regime change. Russia only started to annex land in September 2022 - half a year into the war. The reason was probably that that made it easier to administer the conquered areas. 
 - Keeping Georgia out of the war is a sound strategy from the Georgian point of view. It has nothing to do with how democratic its leaders are.
 - Armenia did not revert to the West after it lost Nagorno Karabach. It did it much earlier. And the sorry fact was that the West did nothing to help it when it was attacked. In the meantime Russia's options were restricted. Armenia had recently refused to do military exercises with Russia and in the diplomatic game around Nagorno Karabach before the war it had followed Western advice and ignored Russia. 
 - It is well known that US propaganda is very active in Kazachstan aiming to turn the public sentiment against Russia. talking with the people it has converted is not a good way to get an impression of the local public opinion.

comments.name: Mark
comments.body:
Russia’s coffers are draining at an increasing rate. Ukraine is making Russians soldier pay in blood and treasure for every small parcel of land the take on the front line. And now Ukrainian drones are striking deep into Russia.

It ‘supporters’ were usually more anti-west than pro Putin, reliant on Russia for cheap energy, food or fertiliser. The neutrals just didn’t want to get involved in a European war. Only Iran and North Korea really helped, and now Iran is busy and Kim is probably being held back by Xi, who is playing the waiting game for Russian land in the east as Putin’s empire declines.

Putin’s problem, after he went mad during Covid, is that like Stalin (and to some degree Trump) he has surrounded himself with people unwilling to tell him truths or very willing to lie. Consequently his understanding of the war is far removed from its reality. 

Russia was always an empire, first with Czars, then with Party Secretaries, and finally with a President (who behaves like a Czar running a Praesidium); but as has happened to all empires, which crumble through overreach or incompetence, it is nearing its end. 

The only strangeness about its predicament is that the man they pinned so much hope on for its continuance has ultimately been the Russian state’s worst bet, not through action but through his absolute and utter incompetence.

comments.name: Mike Iker
comments.body:
I guess that this article is intentionally conflicted, presenting Russia as implacably committed to the war but both widely reviled and supported around the world and probably internally. At this point, viewed through the lens of the Western press, Ukraine seems to be gaining the upper hand on the battlefield, now that the battlefield has expanded to include targets in Russia. But it is still Ukrainian territory that has been seized and much more destruction has occurred in Ukraine than in Russia. And the attrition has a much greater effect in Ukraine, with a much smaller population. 

But I do take the main point, that Russia will not give up. And while Donald Trump doesn’t seem as inclined to betray Ukraine at this point, neither does he seem prepared to support Ukraine militarily, economically or politically. At least he is not actively supporting Russia lately, although with Trump, who knows about the future. But if Russia will not give up, and if they will forever be a danger to Ukraine, then the only way that they will not win in the long term is for them to be defeated militarily. I don’t see how that happens without the USA.

So how with happen? Not while Trump is in office - he really can’t be considered reliable. Under a new administration? That may be a bridge too far. And it might include the realistic risk of a nuclear attack on Ukraine in a “If we can’t have it, nobody can” reaction from Putin or a successor. We didn’t take threat seriously - maybe we should.

comments.name: John
comments.body: Imagine if the US was providing full on military aid to Ukraine to the same extent the EU is now. What a pity. Maybe someday the US will return to the world stage.

comments.name: Phil
comments.body:
Under the Iran war pretext potus removed the sanctions on Russia. Not to mention the drastic cuts in US support for Ukraine. So in a way Putin’s gambles are paying off. Regardless  of his gains in the South. 

The real tragedy is our stable genius has essentially desecrated our country, left our allies, helped in a genocide, provided Iran with a better power leverage and continues to help Putin, not to mention aiding China indirectly, continues to waste billions of dollars in a pointless but economically destructive war even as he lines his family’s pockets with billions, and removed any advantage we had in negotiations in the middle east for ever.

comments.name: eric l.
comments.body: Re Putin's determination to "outlast" the West: It is an uncannily unchanged recycling of Khrushchev's "We will bury you" from some 70 years ago.

articles.title: Putin’s Gamble Might Pay Off
articles.summary: No matter what the West does, Russia will not yield.

comments.name: Richard Donahue
comments.body:
Ho hum, a billion-dollar fine, as if it were a parking ticket.
And the other giant corporations getting fines here and there in the millions, no problem.
And then there is Amazon and Walmart steering employees to government benefits for health care and food.
There are serious problems ahead, and most are just too busy day after day trying to survive, let alone consider what is happening in our democracy.

comments.name: Tired person
comments.body: And this is not essentially the same thing as a tariff.

comments.name: DJS_MI
comments.body:
As the saying goes, if you can’t innovate, regulate. That’s the EU in a nutshell. 

Maybe they should revisit Mario Draghi’s assessment as to how to get European economy back on track.

comments.name: On The Rideau
comments.body:
Bravo to the European Commission. 

This long over due, so please don't bow too Trumpian bluster and pressure.

The longer you hold to your principle of competitive markets, the more heat trump will take at home, and the more likely middle powers outside the EU will replicate your success. Heck, even Canada might revive a digital service tax on Google et al after the Truumpian 50% tax on consumer purchases from Canada comes into effect.

comments.name: rodndtube
comments.body:
Honestly, I am equally or even more appalled by Microsoft's and Apple's behaviors. Apple's closed applesphere makes it difficult to communicate with people using Apple products and in the other direction as well. Microsoft continuously used magic tricks in it promotion of its AI agent and cloud storage and server environment making for an increasingly opaque operating environment.

At this point I am moving slowly but surely to Libre Office Suite to evade some of the pounding by CoPilot and OneDrive.

comments.name: Seal Team Sith
comments.body: Good for Europe.  They know how to stick it to tech barons.  All the major tech giants engage in unfair business practices including Google, Amazon, Meta, X, and Apple.  While our government sleeps, Europe takes action.  Guess Tim Apple got what he wanted when he gave Trump that gold trinket.

comments.name: Hearty
comments.body: I don't doubt that Google has put search results that feature its own products/services at top of the result list.  I would expect to see language translation there for example.  But without giving examples of bias in providing results, I'm not sure what we get out of the article except an opportunity for commenters to bray.

comments.name: Retired
comments.body: Did the EU define for Google what profit level would NOT be abusive to its less capable, less efficient and less productive companies.  US companies are not subject to that kind of central government economic planning by the US government, why should Europe get to be the arbiter of what is acceptable and what is not for US public corporations. They are trying exercise control over a company that exceeds that which even company shareholders have as owners.

articles.title: Google Hit With $1 Billion Fine for Abusing Its Power in Europe
articles.summary: At a tense moment for trans-Atlantic trade, the European Union accused Google of anti-competitive business practices.

comments.name: AH
comments.body:
“Second, in terms of funding, I’d give him even more than he asked for.”

As an average American citizen, I am absolutely sick and tired of the ever increasing military budget and military spending. When are we finally going to focus some meaningful funds on improving the lives of average Americans? When are we finally going to do something about healthcare, education, infrastructure, clean energy, etc.?

comments.name: Tom
comments.body: For years, we've spent around $2 billion per day on our military.  For years, this figure has exceeded the military expenditures of the next 10 or so biggest-spending nations.  The result of this "investment" seems to be a military that is tactically brilliant for warfare as waged in WWII but wholly unsuited to warfare as waged today.  Combined with the strategic misdirection provided by our military planners, our politicians have suffered a shameful absence of competence in the important strategic discipline of choosing when, where, with whom, and for what reasons to wage war.  I wish there could be a quicker solution, but it seems the only option is to vote the war-hawks out of office and then realign our military planners so they build capability for today and tomorrow rather than for warfare waged in decades gone by.  A useful litmus test for military and civil leadership would be one question: Is this candidate a compulsive, pathological liar?

comments.name: Sally
comments.body: I understand that there is a desperate need to rebuild the countries weapon stocks but we need to restore the safety net. By ensuring that all Americans have access to healthy food, housing and health services will ensure that we are a strong nation. And I wouldn't trust this band of fools with my grocery budget. It's a quandary, one I don't have a solution for.

comments.name: Robert O.
comments.body: If we had a competent administration, we would have far less need for huge, incredibly costly stockpiles of munitions. The idea that tariffs can compensate for fiscal irresponsibility over the long-term is ridiculous.

comments.name: Blues

comments.name: Another concerned citizen
comments.body: Understandably the NYT writes for American readers, but focusing only on the travails of tourists in Europe misses the point.  Yesterday AFP reported the excess death toll in France for the month of june was 5,700. 3,000 of those deaths were in the Paris region. So anyone saying that people just need to  get used to the heat is ignoring reality.  I have been in the Montpellier region for over 30 years. We are used to heat here; temps have to be quite high before heatwaves are declared. I can tell you that the heat here since the end of May is awful. I don't have AC and my apartment is an oven. It used to be that without AC one would have a few uncomfortable weeks at the most. That is no longer the case. Traveling here now and trying to do anything besides sitting in the shade or in the water is not a good idea. Yes, more AC is needed. Yes, consider visiting off-season. But what is really needed is action. And the best thing American citizens can do is get rid of Trump and his sychophants and vote in people supporting a Green New Deal. The US is one of the globe's major polluters and U.S. reactionary politics -- in this case in the realm of energy policy and climate skepticism -- are influencing politics in Europe and elsewhere.

comments.name: Fred Edwards
comments.body: It beggars the mind that so many people don't get climate change. These extra toasty temperatures they're a function of greenhouse gases humans already put into the atmosphere. Even if our species went cold turkey on carbon tomorrow, the warming would continue until the atmosphere reaches a new heat equilibrium. But we won't stop, because we love that carbon that comes out of the ground, travels through through pipelines into our houses, businesses, cars and, of course,  the ships and planes that bring us things and take us to all those wonderful, places...and that then ends up in our atmospheric garbage dump.   So those Riyadh summers arriving in Paris and London and the other now appropriately-named  tourist "hotspots," they're coming soon for us, too.  And, as for Riyadh.... imagine....

If you have generous budgets, you could consider also Ireland and Scotland.   For my money, though, the Baltics are more interesting and have better food.

But when they showed Trump on the big screen and the crowd grunted and moan, we felt as cool as a cucumber. My local friend said, "Welcome to RVA!"

comments.name: NYC
comments.body: Maybe a drop in visitor levels is a very good thing. Judging by reporting from this paper, European hotspots (pun intended) are completely overrun w  tourists, now at such high levels, the locals cannot live well in their own cities. I live in a now extremely touristy area in NYC. I can attest to the hideousness of overcrowding, not to mention trash left behind. I feel for locals battling the heat without AC. Tourists, not so much.

comments.name: deborah

A non-infrequent traveler to Western Europe.

Yes, travel is more complicated with global warming (yes indeed, global warming and climate change - global warming precedes as a result of our actions).  Expecting to bring American air conditioning, and (already!!) fast food (don;t eat that - eat local) - you will miss the point of your travel (new experience), unless your point is fancy pictures.
take care out there.  its a beautiful world to see!

comments.name: APS
comments.body: We were in Scotland during the 2022 heatwave, trying to return to London. When temperatures reached 35°C (95°F), train service was suspended because tracks were buckling and road surfaces were melting. Our train effectively abandoned us in the middle of nowhere, with no taxis, vans, or alternative transportation arranged to help passengers reach London, where many of us had accommodations booked. There seemed to be little concern for passengers’ safety or well-being. Fortunately, our compassionate train manager personally arranged a taxi for us later that evening, once the temperature had cooled somewhat. Since then we decided, no more Europe in summer.

comments.name: WB
comments.body: Growing up in the "before times" of the 1960s and 1970s, I would sometimes travel on summer school breaks to visit relatives in southern Switzerland.  There was no air conditioning anywhere, I rarely encountered a fan (no one I knew owned one), there were no window screens, and the heat and humidity could be overwhelming.  My relatives slept under huge mosquito nets, and outdoor dining required all of us to slip into 'potato sacks' to keep swarms of the determined vipers from attacking below table level.  Relief from heat waves was only found at very high elevations, by heading in the opposite direction and plunging into a lake, or when violent overnight thunderstorms cracked through the valleys accompanied by torrential downpours.  As a senior citizen, I wouldn't want to experience those conditions with the temperature now dialed up to "11."

comments.name: AJ
comments.body:
There has been aggressive policies towards fire suppression in the Canadian boreal forest over the last 50 or so years, despite recognition that these forests are adapted to frequent low/moderate severity fires (and indeed need them for their regrowth). Studies suggest that suppression in the boreal has increase fire vulnerability of communities adjacent to these fires.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-15961-y

Clearly however, the shift to hotter and drier summers is driving extreme fire behaviour; fire suppression and fuel buildup in the boreal is a contributing factor. A conflaguration of factors building towards unstoppable fires.

comments.name: Eddie Foley
comments.body:
Are you kidding me?
If we have any chance of adapting, we need a coordinated global
commitment by all governments to move away from a carbon-
based economy.
Even if we went to zero emissions today, the CO2 already
in the atmosphere will continue to make things worse
for at least 50 years.
The situation we are facing now will get much, much worse,
even if our leaders immediately woke up and began working
for the benefit of all of their citizenry and for the survival
of humanity.
Our present government is attempting to erase the physical
realities we all face, and to deny our firm scientific understanding
that clearly indicates we are in the middle of the world's sixth
mass extinction, and climate change represents an existential
threat to humanity.
What this piece suggests is just a band-aid on a wildly
hemorrhaging wound.
A quote from MLK comes to mind:
"We are now faced with the fact that tomorrow is today.
We are confronted with the fierce urgency of now.
In this unfolding conundrum of life and history there is such
a thing as being too late. Procrastination is still the thief of time.
Life often leaves us standing bare, naked, and dejected
with a lost opportunity. The tide in the affairs of men does not
remain at flood — it ebbs. We may cry out desperately for time
to pause in her passage, but time is adamant to every plea
and rushes on. Over the bleached bones and jumbled residues
of numerous civilizations are written the pathetic words,
"Too late."

comments.name: CastleMan

comments.body: Even though we are perfectly able to pay for it, I told my daughter she needed to get a fellowship if she wanted a Ph.D in the liberal arts.  That's because it's incredibly competitive and one needs to know right away if they are up to the challenge.  Graduate programs with a more secure future, such as medicine, might be an exception.  Working for a company that would contribute towards graduate school is another way for this child to put some skin in the game.  I do believe in fairness and in this father contributing something - helping with expenses that a assistantships or fellowships don't cover or a down payment for a house.

comments.name: Kevin

I think grad school should be something you pay for yourself anyway, regardless of your parents' financial situation. 
Undergrad is something you agree to at 17 or 18 with little real understanding of the financial impacts, and most people are expected or even pressured to attend by their parents. So if the parents can help pay for it that's great.

But once you've got the education, you're a few years older... it's time to enter the adult world. Grad school should be something you take on because you have a specific goal, a plan for what to do with the degree, and an understanding of the financial cost/benefit.

comments.name: R C
comments.body:
If you get into a grad program and somehow are paying for anything that isn't room & board, you have essentially not been accepted into the grad program. The intent is for you to take the hint and go get some practical experience before pursuing post-graduate education.

I was paid to attend post-graduate education (via the war college). My parents were handed TA positions as well as financial aid for their graduate educations in the 1970s that resulted in not just covering tuition, but also their living expenses in NYC. My friends who have attended post-grad typically had 70% or more of tuition covered.

The price tag associated with post-graduate education is for over-reachers. People who are going to grad school because "it's a thing," and not because they're ready for it or have a perspective to share with the other post-graduates. I ended up applying to a post-grad program in an engineering specialty at 38. The admin and the school's dean threw money at me because they wanted the perspective of someone with 20 years of experience across military, public and private sector in the courses.

If you're not feeling like the carpet was rolled out for you as a grad student, it may be time to consider real work experience.

comments.name: Tom Debley

One passage in this analysis deserves our deepest attention: the suggestion that commercial interests may be taking precedence over long-standing nuclear nonproliferation safeguards.

What kind of world are we preparing for our children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren? If restraints on uranium enrichment and international inspections are weakened, are we helping to ignite a new nuclear arms race in one of the world's most volatile regions?

The United States bears a unique moral responsibility. We remain the only nation ever to have used atomic weapons against cities. Hiroshima and Nagasaki should have taught us that humanity now possesses the capacity for mass killing on a scale that challenges every moral principle developed over centuries of thinking about war.

No commercial agreement is valuable enough to justify weakening barriers against nuclear proliferation. Before moving forward, Americans should ask one more question: Is this the right administration to be reshaping the global nuclear order? Given President Trump's record of impulsive decision-making and the advisers around him, that is not a partisan question. It is a question of responsibility to future generations.

“Like everyone on the tour of Ausable Chasm, a gorge carved into the Adirondacks in upstate New York, I wore a harness to catch me if I fell. Maybe it would save my life, but it didn’t do much to ease my anxiety.”

The operators of Adventure Trail and the manufacturers of the gear they use are counting on that gear saving you with 100% surety. The engineering involved in a via ferrata is also designed and maintained to that end. 

The real test for ability to handle heights is to move easily in an exposed position without any of the engineering or safety equipment. As a rock climber of 50+ years I marvel at the photos of old school iron workers casually moving around hundreds of feet in the air, working, eating lunch, whatever.

I recommend the author take the next step and actually go rock climbing with a good guide. Using the actual natural features of a climbing introduces a different and more meaningful challenge from a via ferrata that may distract you from your fear.

The climbing area known as the Shawangunks, near New Paltz, has a famous route called High Exposure. Its last pitch puts the climber 300 feet above the forest over plenty of air, albeit on easy climbing. As a teenager I free soloed it from bottom to top, never having climbed it before. I am confident I wouldn’t do that now, but on a rope I am confident it would not be too big a deal.

comments.name: Laurel
comments.body: That so many people were affected by the cyclospora outbreak purportedly tied to a single [albeit huge] farm, exposes the issues inherent with concentrating large portions of our food supply into a few producers or farms, where a single misalignment can affect thousands. Foods from these farms are transported in large quantities over long distances and they reach many more markets than ever before, and they're also processed into many end products such as single-serve or institutional-sized packaged salad mixes that have overtaken the produce sections all across our country and are often mixed with other lettuces, which can make them harder to trace than if they were sold whole to wholesalers and supermarkets. So even one problem in the chain along the way in the growing, handling, packaging, refrigeration, and distribution can easily cascade into widespread illness and even deaths and result in massive recalls and loss of wages and livelihoods for many. But the most widespread damage is the loss of confidence in our food suppliers and in the regulatory committees whose job it is to monitor and maintain the health and integrity of our food supply. Our country’s health leaders cannot be urging Americans to be healthy and to eat more fresh fruits and vegetables if it cannot adequately monitor all the actors in our increasingly vast and complex food supply network.

No idea where this outbreak is coming from but it's way too easy to blame Mexico, they are not alone. Taylor Farms and other big growers also have major produce farms in the U.S. 

It's worth watching the 2023 Netflix documentary, "Poisoned: The Dirty Truth About Your Food". Large livestock operations near produce farms likely continue to be a major source of outbreaks. Much of the documentary focus is on poultry farms and high salmonella risks but they also mention a couple of major known growing areas like Salinas Valley, CA and Yuma, AZ (where Taylor farms also operates). These areas create major contamination risks and I'm sure there are many more. Animal waste contains harmful pathogens like E. coli and many others. Irrigation systems, runoff and wind and dust soil movement carry the pathogens from nearby livestock operations that settle directly onto plants before harvest. These long known risks need to addressed. I'm not against big produce farms but they should not be anywhere near big livestock farming operations and all food should be easily traceable so when contamination is identified it can be quickly contained.

In summer and fall, I buy and support local growers. Winter I tend to eat less produce and select more frozen produce from lower risk growers without a recall history.

comments.name: Sarah
comments.body:
I am a biologist who teaches cell biology at a medical school. The term “peptide” just means a short chain of amino acids connected to each other with peptide bonds.

Some peptides are antimicrobial (kill bacteria). Some peptides are structural building blocks. Some peptides break down clots. Some enhance pain sensation. Many peptides are signaling molecules; meaning, cells use them to communicate with each other and to initiate chemical reactions and physiological changes.

The peptides these people want to sell and inject are hormones (signaling molecules that affect cells far away in the body). Most peptide hormones have more than one function and affect more than one type of cell. Some peptide hormones can stimulate normal cells and cancer cells in the same way, and some have different effects on healthy cells and pathological cells.

We do not know all the cells and tissues that are affected by these 7 peptides, or all of their functions (what reactions or chain reactions they trigger). As the article notes, the data are muddled by a lack of consistency in formulations. Meaning, vendors use the same name for different chemical variations, doses, and delivery methods.

Perhaps if we called these peptides “experimental hormones”, or better yet, “experimental hormones whose functions are not well understood”, maybe more people would understand why scientists and physicians want more research done before they are approved as medicine.

I spent most of 2011 in Kandahar as a Navy doc treating wounded NATO forces, ANA (Afghan Nat Army), Taliban and Afghan civilians.
The ANA were pretty pathetic soldiers, most of them had an opium habit, very demanding and difficult to treat. My Taliban patients struck me as being stoic, polite and respectful. One knew immediately they believed in their cause. 
Also worth noting is the Taliban took care of their wounded better than the Afghan government did. The Taliban would risk capture and drop their most seriously wounded at our front gate knowing we would give them top notch care their medics couldn't. However there was at least one wounded Afghan soldier who was starved to death at the Afghan government hospital in Kabul since he had no family or money to bribe the staff to bring him food!
When you have more respect for your enemy than your supposed allies in a foreign conflict you are doomed to lose the war. I have heard similar sentiments expressed by Vietnam vets comparing the skill and motivation of the North Vietnamese Army vs the very corrupt South Vietnam govt. and mostly incompetent ARVN.

I was 19 when I enlisted in Fall 1966. I was just a scared college kid who believed the war in Vietnam was right but, like most kids my age, I'd rather be home and back in college dating girls.  By the time I was 22 I was totally disillusioned.  The great majority of the college kids I enjoyed as friends were vehemently against the war. Even though by 1970 I understood the war was a catastrophic loss I would not join in protests as I believed those protests encouraged the North to continue the war and would lengthen it rather than bring everyone home sooner.  I still believe I was right about that.  I also believe politicians greatly contributed to continuing in a lost cause until 1975.  We never should have been in Vietnam. 
Years later we engaged in a war against Iraq, then Afghanistan and now against Iran and the Houthis of Yemen.  And again, I strongly believe these were chosen wars except the original battle to topple the Taliban after 911.  Osama bin Laden and his Taliban supporters would have continued to attack the United States homeland again and again.  So, they had to be destroyed.  
Now Donald Trump believes, wrongly, that Iran had to be attacked to force their capitulation and ending their nuclear arms programs.  But, in fact Iran was going along with agreement signed by the Obama administration.  
Trump hid from service in Vietnam.  Now he's commander in chief in a bloody, unending, and unraveling war against Iran. 
He knows nothing.  We should all know better.

comments.body:
This discussion could go beyond chaff to discuss radar-confounding coatings. I believe the author’s company in fact makes some of these coatings. At one end of the spectrum are the military’s proprietary coatings used on stealth vehicles, and at the other end we find some consumer level coatings. Of course, radars use specific frequency sensitivity and different frequencies for different kinds of targets. It’s a serious challenge to defeat them.

Teaming a decoy laden with chaff with a coatings-enhanced prime delivery vehicle could improve chances of penetration; said chaff decoy could carry more material if not burdened with a weapons payload.

For structural and residential uses, specialized coatings like WOREMOR RF-IE50 (available at Home Depot for about $93) utilize carbon fibers rather than graphite to block high-frequency electromagnetic (5G/RF) fields from entering rooms. Companies such as MWT Materials offer commercial variants like the MF-500 Urethane coating, which are compounded with magnetic nano-powders for broad-frequency microwave attenuation.

I wouldn't be surprised if Ukraine isn't also working on small burst transmitters as a way to confuse targeting.

I would hope that the US makes its classified coatings available to Ukraine although that would require careful decisions by an administration that is careless.

This piece, as others have noted, is a glorified advert that has no place in the WSJ editorial section.

comments.name: Look Ahead
comments.body:
Two points usually missed about NAFTA:

It was negotiated in the mid-1990s, at a time of economic disaster in Mexico, the peso devaluation crisis. I saw the shuttered factories firsthand, including our own that supplied the Mexico market. Without NAFTA, Mexico was at risk of becoming a failed state on our southern border (see “Cuba and Venezuela emigration”). NAFTA saved Mexico. 

Prior to NAFTA, Mexico had a highly protectionist regime. After NAFTA, our Mexico plant became a leader in flexible manufacturing, even while our US and Canadian plant volumes grew apace. NAFTA quadrupled US-Mexico trade in both directions. European and Asian automakers built assembly plants in the US, supplied by parts makers in Mexico. 

But our President was making TV shows at the time, so apparently knows nothing of this.

comments.name: Mark Kropf
comments.body:
There is a native capacity for humans to develop which is often unappreciated.    Surrogate factors are used to define this or that segment by the way of skin pigmentation or skull form at times and the nature of Nazi collections of skulls for the analysis was popular to show the 'Aryan' superiority.

Stephen Jay Gould wrote the Mismeasure of Man which is also worth reading for its correction of what was one of the dead ends of prejudicial thinking of the past.

We need to see capacity as something hardly limited to this individual or that.    Humans can all excel if given the right circumstances so long as they suffer no genetic or developmental fault (not a racial one here but a true chromosomal or gene fault!) and no toxic exposure.

Even animals are more capable than we consider.   Researchers in my days of undergraduate education took it for granted that only humans had language.

We now speak of languages of whales, of great apes, of Parrots and Corvids (crows and ravens), of Elephants and of Prarie Dogs.

What we presume we know is what we have convinced ourselves that we understand.   Collective stupidity is often the nature of some holding of prejudice seeking a result it may determine by the nature of what it seeks to define as a criteria for capability.

Intelligence, when all is said and done, needs open-minded assessment of how it is measured and understood as even defined.

comments.name: Frank Knarf

The other pole of this perpetual fight against reactionary fantasies of divine right is the left-populist illiberalism that rejects expertise, believes against evidence in the "blank slatism" that becomes the "new man", celebrates the lived experience of the "wretched of the Earth" while sneering at "white" epistemology based on reason and mirrors the unhinged right populism that has produced the oligarchicalTrump administration. A functioning, just, modern society depends on the work of a technocratic layer that is demonstrably elite in a pragmatic sense. Ancestry is irrelevant. What matters is the ideological character and integrity of the political leadership chosen by the populace, whether one sees a nation of solid citizens or a mob. Allowing the DSA to redefine the structure that brought us here may not be the best approach. Liberal reform is slow and boring, but revolution usually gets us the "new boss".

comments.name: History Guy
comments.body:
All humans are human but that's where Jefferson's notion of "equal" ends. 

IQ scores are real as are SAT scores, with a very small cultural bias. Very small. And they are outstanding predictors of future success.

So is the ability to focus and adhere to personal discipline and tenacity, with professional athletes being classic examples. They may not score all that well on an SAT but they have an emotional intelligence that guides their actions.

Still, there's honest questions to be asked about why some large populations of people seem to be forever struggling and forever behind.

Elon Musk believes it's race. As does Trump and his group, led by Stephen Miller. They're not even trying to hide it. 

I don't know what Americans believe over all, but it's perhaps instructive that Trump has won the white vote in his three presidential runs to the remarkable tune of 60%.

He explained the idea in his 1903 essay, "The Talented Tenth"  and supported/promoted the idea for his entire life.

After reading dozens of depressing news stories in today's Times, I was cheered to see a piece about my adoptive home-town, Bangkok.

Bangkok is a wonderful place to live or to visit. The ferry along the Chaopraya will provide a very full day of entertainment with stops at ICON SIAM, Wat Phra Kaew, Wat Pho, Wat Arun, The Royal Palace, and Chinatown. Tour of the Jim Thomson House is excellent. Chatuchak Park weekend market is great if you like heat and crowds, but Tues - Thurs is the plant market which is a must visit for plant lovers. The shopping malls here can be a lot of fun. I like the three interconnected malls EM Quartier, EMSphere and the Emporium. And wonderful public parks like Benjasiri, Benjaketti, and Lumphini, not to mention my local park Santipap... just be careful not to step on the water monitors that wander freely.

Personally, I cannot imagine a visit to Bangkok without seeing the Nana Entertainment Complex with three floors of clubs, each offering a specialty... spanking, bondage, ladyboys, etc. An important part of the Bangkok experience.

I would not particularly recommend Phuket (it's okay). Much better to visit the group of islands Koh Samui (White Lotus), Koh Phangan, and Koh Tao (amazing diving and snorkeling).

I was totally floored by John Wogan's suggestion (companion article) of a low priced option in Chiang Rai costing $320/night. Very strange notion of low cost. You can stay in wonderful hotels in Thailand for cheap.

comments.name: Estefania Caldissimo 2.0

My free counsel to Mr. Federov, born of a lifetime studying military history, is Voltaire's famous quote: "Don't let the perfect be the enemy of the good".

Iterative progress 'failing forward' is better than stalled, self-righteous Perfectionism which precludes pragmatism, compromise or common sense.
Ukraine's army is stronger with Federov overseeing things in any capacity; so he shouldn't get caught up in the semantics of rank, title or whether he's technically Defense Minister.
History will vindicate his efforts.

The case of US army general Patton during WW2 is a useful analogy; temperamentally egotistical, he was resentful of being subordinated to his former junior officer, Omar Bradley.
But as the ingenious operational whiz of the 3rd army, Patton achieved more glory destroying the German army than Eisenhower, Marshall or other paper-pushers who outranked him.

Federov appears most efficacious as a catalyst "force multiplier"; whose presence in processes/policies yields better results than if his innovation is sidelined.
Institutional changes can be slow and unwieldy, though; so having lodged his complaints, it's time for Federov to move on productively and accept the things he cannot change yet (with the wisdom to know the difference).
