comments.name: Jordan
comments.body: India is a Paper Tiger. I recently visited and enjoyed it immensely — obviously saw less than a fraction of a large and diverse country — but in my 2 weeks there I observed what many other Western visitors do: a stark contrast between the haves and the have-nots, immense poverty, a fully intact ancient caste system, and pollution of a magnitude that is unfathomable. The wealthy isolate themselves in modern Western subdivisions while the majority try to just eke out a minimal viable living. Most everyone I encountered would gladly move to the US if they had a path to living here instead. The Cockroach party was just transitioning from satire to full on movement when I was there. Not sure what they will accomplish but I do hope for a brighter future for the subcontinent and its bright, friendly, and hopeful people of all ages. The environmental challenge alone would be a good starting point that could generate jobs and set a vital foundation for real progress at a larger and more equitable scale.

comments.body: As someone who attended the same secondary school as Charles Rennie Mackintosh, studied at the Glasgow School of Art for four years and even got married in his Queens Cross Church. Words cannot adequately describe how heartbreaking this dreadful loss is.

comments.name: Peter
comments.body: There comes a point where it is madness to throw good money after bad and allowing the premises to burn down twice indicates that we have reached that point with this building. The Glasgow School of Art is a living, vibrant institution and money should now be spent to create a home for it that meets the needs of a 21st century art college. Spending vast amounts of money to recreate something that would inevitably be a pastiche of the original does not serve well the needs of today's students. Scotland does not lack fine, historic buildings. What it does lack are modern public buildings of real architectural merit. Should the Glasgow School of Art not set an example by commissioning a contemporary Scottish architect to design a landmark building for this age.

comments.name: Kemlo Yaris
comments.body: I was fortunate to visit the School of Art as a tourist shortly before the first devastating fire. I am not an obvious person to be blown away by art or architecture but my hour or so in this building affected me in a way that no other building ever has done. I came away with an understanding of what great architecture means, not just bricks and mortar but the creation and expression of a coherent vision down to the last detail including everything from furniture to light fittings to door handles. If even I could come away in an hour thinking "I get it now!" then the value of this building to future young architects is incalculable and transcends politics. This is Scotland's Notre Dame and needs to be rebuilt.

comments.name: South Florida
comments.body: I was incredibly fortunate to have been able to work in Scotland at Hawthornden Castle, a retreat for writers and other artists outside Edinburgh, and I went to Mackintosh's  Glasgow School of Art before the first fire in 2014. I think it's almost impossible for anybody who has ever been in it not to be aware of its beauty and power and the quiet Beauty of its uniquely detailed interior. I have a picture in my home in the States of the Library, and I told a recent visitor who studied the image that it felt like a holy place. It occurs to me that if everybody who read about the situation prevailing for the school right now gave a single dollar, from every country in which this sort of article appears, in their currency, that would be millions of single dollars and they would add up and it might be possible to repair the building. This is the kind of thing that sounds child- like, but I wonder if the Scottish government would handle such an event, advertising and collecting the funds that would pour in if various newspapers in 50 countries asked their citizens to contribute that very small amount in their own currency.  I hope this strikes a chord in others who would happily donation very small funds. It would take a lot of donations, but there are lots of art lovers in the world. Let's go, y'all!

As far as monies, start collecting from every Scot even a few pence at a time, and telegraph the need for funds to all the Scottish descendants around the world. Go to all the Lairds and ask for a contribution, beg, borrow and if necessary, “ steal”, as this is a treasure that cannot be allowed to slowly disintegrate and become a ruin. comments.name: Robert D. Stolorow
comments.body:
Catastrophic Wildfires and Apocalyptic Anxiety

Robert D. Stolorow

     Living in the Bay Area near San Francisco, I am far from the catastrophic wildfires that have been assaulting Los Angeles and the neighboring communities. Despite this long distance, I have been feeling an uncanny sense of danger, an anxiety that often appears in my body in the form of physical pain. The anxiety bears a similarity to my descriptions of reactions to the horrors of climate change, what I called “Apocalyptic anxiety” (Stolorow, 2024). 

     Such anxiety announces not only the loss of individual lives but also the destruction of human civilization itself, the nullifying of all future human possibilities. It thereby signals the ending of the historical process through which we make sense of our individual existences. Apocalyptic anxiety is thus often accompanied by a gripping sense of meaninglessness, a profound nihilism. “What’s the point?” is a refrain I can imagine haunting the rubble of the LA wildfires.

     I have previously discussed the use of metaphysical illusion to evade the catastrophic  consequences of climate change—specifically, the view of the earth as an indestructible and timeless metaphysical entity. A common way of evading the Apocalyptic anxiety evoked by the catastrophic wildfires is blame.  Blaming, especially as practiced by certain politicians, replaces powerlessness and vulnerability with aggression and illusory prosecutory power.

comments.name: Walt
comments.body: Amidst all this chaos and sorrow, there is one bright spot of which NYT readers should be aware. This is the Hospital Albert Schweitzer in Haiti’s Artibonnite Valley. Begun 60+ years ago by Larry Mellon and his wife and still supported by the Pittsburgh-based Mellon Foundation, this incredibly durable and resilient institution continues to provide high-level medical care and public health assistance to thousands of Haitians every year. I volunteered for four months as a physician there some years ago and can affirm that every dollar received is used to maximal benefit. Now, with murderous gangs at their very doorstep, the brave staff of HAS continue to provide critically needed care at great personal risk and sacrifice. There is little any of can do about the larger problems detailed in this depressing article (beyond writing letters etc.), but we can directly support Haitians in need through support of HAS. Donations are handled here in the US by the Mellon Foundation.

But I can't help but wonder about the insulating properties of glass bricks. The R-factor (resistance to thermal transmission) must be very low. I I would use glass bricks (or their look-alike, but lighter, cousins, acrylic bricks) for interior partitions, and for small windows, but not for entire exterior walls. But then, I live in the far north, where affordably keeping a house warm in the winter requires a multidisciplinary strategy. We can't change the winter cold; we can do little to ameliorate the rising prices of various heating energy sources; but we can design and build to retain heat.

comments.body: I loved the character of Lestat and the actor playing him. Here was the problem: the writers focused on Lestat's backstory, always flashing back to moments in history, rather than moving the story forward. It seemed to get worse as the season went on, until we spent the entire last episode -- promised to be the climax with the big "concert" -- wallowing in past slights, aggressions, disappointments, betrayals, with an assemblage of extraneous characters that are no longer very central to the story.  Enough with the references to the past "coven" and whatever happened in Paris. The delight of the show is in watching Lestat navigate the modern world, seeing how he chooses to spend his immortal time and manipulate those around him. Lestat needs to meet a new love interest, perhaps a human this time. He needs to explore and exploit his rock star persona. Maybe he moves to Hollywood and decides to be a movie star next season?  In any case, he needs to move FORWARD.

comments.name: Hannah
comments.body:
I'm glad that the main thrust of this article seems to be that Sam Reid is giving an absolutely incredible performance as Lestat, because that is really true. Through all three seasons but especially in the last couple episodes of season 2 and in this season, it's one of the most astonishing performances I've ever seen. He's genuinely a great actor, and he and Jacob Anderson (who is also an incredible actor, as you said) are pure magic together. I know awards are not the measure of quality and genre shows often have a tougher time, but I'd love his performance to get some awards attention. 

But overall, I strongly disagree with this. I haven't read the book, so I can't speak to it as an adaptation, but I found the season to be a really powerful, layered, nuanced examination of how trauma lives in a person, and Lestat is an incredible complex character. Season 3, where he drops his guard enough to be honest about Nicki, and then we see him really reckon with the horror of his experience with Magnus (isn't the point of the pop song retelling that it's not the truth, it's him coping?); episode 5, where we see so much innocence and whimsy in him before yet another traumatizing experience; episode 6, where we see him break down the way he does and he and Louis have such intimate, beautiful, honest conversations with each other....I just feel there's so much more to the show than this review conveys, as different as it and Lestat are from the first two (great) seasons.

comments.name: N.G. Krishnan
comments.body:
Beijing’s strategy of leveraging open-weight A.I. models to engineer global technological reliance reflects a mindset that tactical cunning is strategic genius. Much like a grand Ponzi scheme, it yields rapid, visible dominance by borrowing heavily against future trust—until the inevitable reckoning arrives.

History is littered with autocratic systems that mistook early compliance for permanent submission.

Blinded by the illusion of their own infallibility, Beijing’s leaders seem to have forgotten that overreach generates the exact counter-pressures that undermine it.

By threatening to restrict model access, China hasn't sealed its supremacy; it has exposed its hand. 

Rather than reacting with hasty bans, outsiders should step in with their own dependable, open-weight A.I. infrastructure—proving once again that open ecosystems will always outlast autocratic leverage.

comments.name: N.G. Krishnan
comments.body:
China’s playbook of using open-weight A.I. models to build global dependence—a tactic straight from its solar, telecom, and rare-earth supply chain manoeuvres is exposed. 

But it rests on a fundamental miscalculation: assuming that aggressive leverage won't provoke an equal and opposite reaction.

In the Mahabharata, the ancient Indian epic, there is a recurring truth: power and intellect unguided by humility act as a ticking time bomb—the grander the ego, the harder the fall. 

China’s calculated attempt to trap the world’s developer ecosystem on its models, only to suddenly pull back the curtain and restrict access, exemplifies this short-sighted hubris.

By threatening to sequester its latest models, Beijing is not securing permanent supremacy; it is simply ringing the alarm bell for the rest of the world.

The outside world must seize this opening, not with reactionary bans, but by building and funding an open, reliable, and secure A.I. foundation that global builders can actually trust. 

China’s ploy may be cunning, but history shows that overreach inevitably creates the very opposition that dismantles it.

It is a fact that the majority of its incumbent political establishment (Liberal Democratic Party - LDP) are direct descendants of samurai-turned-politicians from that time. Abe's maternal grandfather, Nobusuke Kishi, a prime minister himself from 1957-1960, served in the war cabinet of imperial Japan and was a paramount founding member of the LDP. 

Compared with Germany and Italy, which at least criminalized  Nazism and Fascism, Japan did not do the same thing. Figures like Mr. Abe and Ms. Takaichi are likely to continue emerging as long as Japan does not genuinely break from the past. There is uncertainty if it is possible.

The best fashion designers, of course, respond to societal shifts and moods to make clothing that expresses those shifts and moods. What fun it was to see Bobbi's 70s and 80s era reporting. She was a skilled anthropologist! She was the first to cover Donna Karan's debut collection in 1984: casually-comfy yet sexy pieces that women could wear to work and beyond. They still look fresh! But I had never heard of The Skimp, which apparently was a minidress invented by Halston in 1974. (Bobbi wrote that a proper Skimp was between 32 and 34 inches long.) Halston's sold for $260 (more than $1,700 in today's dollars) but, as Bobbi noted, department stores sold their own versions for $11. But do any of you who are "of age" remember a Skimp? It was news to me!

When the so-called city editor, a man I called Si, passed around one of my articles to staff soon to be published  as an example of sloppy copy to be avoided, with crossed out words, etc, Bobbi stood up and announced, loudly for all to hear. "Oh Si, that's mean! If somebody did that to me, I'd cry." Si took back my sloppy copy and I knew Bobbi Queen personified a rare breed in this world.

comments.name: Laurel
comments.body:
I love her hair! Looking at Ms. Galli's hair is a reminder of how important it is for people with naturally curly/wavy hair to have a stylist who specializes in these hair types. 

I have a mixture of naturally curly/wavy hair. It wasn't always like that; I began getting curls around puberty, oddly. I blow dried it straight for years. Then about 20 years ago I decided to work with what I have. The largest struggle has been to find someone who knows how to cut and style natural curls and not leave me with the dreaded triangle-shaped hair. I've lived in several places in the last 24 years and I went through a few stylists before finding someone. Recently I found someone after only a year who specializes only in curls. She's a two hour drive from me, but she cuts it so well, it keeps its shape about four months (I've gone six), so worth the commute. I recently had my hair cut while on a road trip (I didn't have time to cut it before I left) and I found someone along the route with experience with curls and she also did a fantastic job. So I urge anyone having trouble getting the right cut to look for someone who specializes in curls/waves, or just try one to see the difference. I didn't know they existed. It has totally transformed my hair and my confidence, and I haven't had a bad hair day in a long time. My husband says the new cuts elevate my personality, give me a more exuberant look. He's very honest with feedback, too much so sometimes! so I'm careful with what I ask him!

Communication breaks down quickly in even the best of scenarios. Add an extreme event like fire, flood, hurricane and you really are on own-in a heartfelt finger snap. 

Information is sketchy. Outdated. Just plain wrong.

I recall the wrap up of the 2012 Costa Concordia cruise ship disaster. 

Guests received little instruction.  Worse, most of what was transmitted was conflicting.  Some donned life vests while others sought info. 

There are photos of the list of the ship, guests standing knee deep in water. 

Have a plan. You are on your own.

comments.name: George Dog
comments.body:
I suspect that when the smoke has cleared that we may find that staff in Northern Ontario had to clear all external notifications, such as forest fire evacuation notices through their Head office in Toronto. The politicians and their senior staff are terrified of stepping over the line and always seek more senior authorization for public notices. This then resulted in hand wringing and delay or even failure to act. We increasingly see this desire at the top to control the message and to now blame the Federal Government for a local issue.

What we have seen in the past 20 years is an increasing lack of understanding of the geography and indigenous issues in Northern Ontario, although knowledge was never great. It is 1.5 hours by jet airplane from Toronto to Thunder Bay and then up to a 10 + hour drive to get to the end of the road depending where you are going. The view in the south is that 'the north' is a few hours drive from Toronto. There is little understanding of the size of the Province - about the size of Texas + Oklahoma and most of Kansas with few roads. Or France + Germany + Belgium and Holland.

When I mentored engineering staff for the Transportation Dept I would ensure that they got some understanding of  the northern issues by exposure through site visits and sometimes secondments. Unfortunately I doubt that is happening so easily today with an increasingly stingy attitude toward staff development and lack of appreciation of the geography.

comments.name: Ron T.
comments.body:
When their were major rains and flooding in Estes Park, Colorado in 2014, our clueless town administrator at the time claimed that everything people needed to know would be on the town's Facebook page.  The trouble was: much of the town was without power, and fiber optic lines and telephone lines (remember DSL?) had been ripped out by the flooding, and there was no way for anyone to get any information!   We did have an AM radio station decades before then, but it went off the air a good quarter century ago, with the antenna taken down and sold as scrap.
NEVER trust social media to be a source of information when you need it!

comments.name: RC
comments.body: How long you live is obviously important but I'm not sure that quantity of life is worth sacrificing quality of life. My 90 year old grandfather, who was born and grew up in Sicily, had a glass of wine (or two) pretty much every day of his life. He already ate about as Mediterranean a diet as a person possibly could but he did like a glass of wine to go with his meals, typically the wine that he made himself. When diabetes started getting the better of him as he got older his doctors urged to cut out all alcohol so he asked them what would be the benefit if he stopped drinking wine. They told him there was no assurance that anything would change but likely he would feel better and live a little bit longer. He told them thank you for your advice but I feel okay and I've lived long enough and he kept on having a glass of wine with his meals for the rest of his life, dying in his sleep one night at 96. Healthy choices are not simply limited to what we eat but also to how we live our lives.

I am struggling with something similar. My father was hard on me and our lives were tough. Our weekends were spent pulling weeds and working around the yard. We got hit sometimes nightly just for talking to my sisters before falling asleep, and we were always on his schedule. He was there at home after work and on weekends but tasks and work around the house always took priority. I would call him an absent father during my childhood and my niece, his granddaughter recently said that she feels nothing for him. He wasn’t there for his grandchildren either except for the few summers he’d cart them around in a trailer behind a tractor when they visited. 

My father is 83 and has been recently diagnosed with Alzheimer’s. He’s with me a day or two a week so my mom can get away for a bit. He sleeps mostly then I make him lunch. I catch myself looking at him a lot and wonder why he is so different now. He’s quiet and gentle, he’s appreciative of his pb&j or fried egg sandwich I make him and he’s able to carry on a good conversation most days. So comes the feelings for this man, my dad. Looking at him you’d never know he used to hit kids. I’m having trouble separating the two different men at two different times in their lives. He’s just different now.

comments.body:
To put some context on why these events are happening, just look at measured CO2 concentration in Earth's atmosphere from over a hundred years to recently:

year: CO2 concentration (mean)

1900: 294 ppm

1919: 302 ppm

1940: 308 ppm

1960: 317 ppm

1980: 339 ppm

2000: 370 ppm

2020: 414 ppm

2024: 425 ppm

Because humans burn over a 100 million barrels of oil every single day (plus all the coal, and natural gas), 
the CO2 from the burning all those fossil fuels accumulates 
(it takes a very long time to come out of the atmosphere, unlike methane).

And as CO2 concentration increases, Earth's average temperature increases (as does the ocean temperature).

And more importantly: for every one degree Celsius that Earth’s atmospheric temperature rises, the amount of water vapor the atmosphere can hold increases by about 7% 
(from Clausius–Clapeyron relation in thermodynamics). 

That means that a given parcel of air can suck up more moisture 
(and if not released right away) 
causes droughts; 

or,
 
if atmospheric forcing causes a sudden release: 
major flooding 
(like in the July 2025 Texas floods that killed a bunch of children). 

And as ocean temperatures rise, evaporation increases, and any "atmospheric river" flooding events that form become more intense.

Even worse is that hurricanes can become stronger and rapidly intensify.

This extreme weather will only get worse and worse.

We need to stop burning fossil fuels: adapting will get harder and more expensive.

comments.name: George S.
comments.body:
What concerns me about reports such as this it that they are agenda driven and seek evidence to support a preconceived finding.

Yes, I do not doubt that climate change is both real and is likely to contribute to infrastructure damage and the high costs of repairs.

But the reality is over the next 24 years much of the infrastructure now seen at risk would require repair and replacement anyway.

Things get old and often, when they do, ultimately fall apart.

The contention that we are even capable of identifying what infrastructure would remain sound except for climate change is really unsupportable.

A more responsible analysis would be that in accepting that climate change will likely worsen and have a greater deleterious effect we should further "harden" infrastructure when repairs and replacement become necessary.

The reality remains that NY will have to spend many billions of dollars for infrastructure repair even without the negative effects of climate change.  

The final reality is that, like it or not, due to age and perhaps accelerated by climate change, NY is going to have to spend billions on infrastructure repairs and replacements.

The challenge then become one of exactly how current and future generations are going to pay for it?

What worries me in particular about these fires is that they are turning our forests from important carbon sinks into net emitters of carbon dioxide (CO2, a greenhouse gas).

The 2023 Canadian wildfires released more CO2 than the rest of Canadian sources combined (37 million acres burned). Climate models did not project fires like that until much later this century.

And recently this paper reported that the permafrost region has shifted from an important carbon sink into a net emitter of greenhouse gases, CO2 and methane.

Some natural systems like forests and frozen soils which minimized some of the impacts of our atmospheric experiment with our only planet are changing from being our friends to our enemies.

There is a profound difference between the situation in the Red Sea and the situation in the Strait of Hormuz. In the Red Sea region, U.S. allies already maintain active, ongoing naval deployments, primarily tasked with countering Houthi strikes on ships and regional maritime threats. They have maintained a significant naval presence there for years and operate under coalition frameworks.

Furthermore, the Iranian leadership likely recognizes that it would be wise to keep distance from the Houthis, as Iran could find itself in a precarious position if it coordinates with the Houthis on attacks against civilian ships and allied navies in the Red Sea. In my view, threats to blockade the Red Sea by the Houthis will prove to be ineffective and unsuccessful for those reasons, notwithstanding the media’s efforts to sensationalize the developments in the Red Sea and tie them to the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict.

Nevertheless, based on my observations, I got the feeling that the institutional traders - and perhaps even private bettors - might be gearing up to use any news of an initial attack in the Red Sea as an opportunity, a cover, or a justification to create profitable volatility and benefit from it.

In any case, the administration should consider imposing a special wartime windfall tax on all such activities of financial institutions and prediction markets as well as oil and gas companies that profit excessively from the conflict and the resulting energy market volatility.

To explain why NewJeans mattered, success alone is not enough. K-pop was increasingly built around maximalism: huge drops, overstuffed concepts and songs designed to announce themselves instantly. NewJeans made restraint feel revolutionary. Their best records—“Attention,” “Hype Boy,” “Ditto,” “OMG” and “Super Shy”—were light, melodic and rhythmically subtle, drawing on 1990s and early-2000s R&B, UK garage and club music without sounding like museum pieces. Their voices worked as a group texture rather than a competition for the biggest note, while their videos made youth, friendship and ordinary life more vivid than another elaborate fictional universe.

My own K-pop hierarchy has BigBang and Blackpink as the two greatest groups, with Teddy Park’s production important to both. NewJeans would have deserved third place had their career not been interrupted and had they maintained that standard while developing. They had barely begun. The tragedy is not merely the music we missed, but the artistic growth that was arrested.

A great group changes without losing its identity. NewJeans appeared capable of that. A return without Danielle, and perhaps without the creative team that shaped them, cannot simply recreate 2022. But it is not too late. I hope everyone involved understands that NewJeans was not a formula or a name: it was a rare alignment of members, songs, production and visual imagination. Preserve that, and they may again release the best music in K-pop.

Brooklyn Botanic Garden made a poor choice. 

As a trustee for a non-profit, I'm shocked she was even considered. Sue Donoghue played a pivotal role in protecting Eric Adams while Trump's DOJ was moving to dismiss Adams' corruption charges. Her conduct as Parks Commissioner was shameful and demonstrated that she has neither the strength or ethical fortitude to lead such a prominent NYC institution.

articles.title: She Knows Parks, and Now She’ll Run a Famous Garden

comments.name: Colenso
comments.body:
'IVORY: I drive S.U.V.s myself. I have kids; we need space.'

With due respect, this doesn't add up. Families used to be larger than today. 

In the fifties, a large family could squeeze into a station wagon. Not just in the USA, in Oz, NZ, the UK,

A-pillars back then were generally much narrower than today. 

A-pillars have widened in order to impart more structural strength and stiffness to the cabin, partly to improve safety in case of a rollover, by preventing the roof from collapsing.

Most cars in 50s were less powerful than today. They were also much more fun to drive. Automatics hadn't yet replaced stick shifts. Driving fast was a greater test of skill.

Today, cars are just auolmated giant boxes on wheels with aircon and entertainment systems stuffed in.

Very few drivers today, outside racing drivers, cab drivers, haulage drivers, construction drivers, et al, are as skilled as many amateur drivers were in the 50s.

comments.body: For those of us in central California, a summer temperature of 104+ is known as "a standard day in July or August." Don't get me wrong, it's still hellishly hot, we just don't have a special word for it. (OK, once it his 108 or so, I tend to just say "repulsive.")

articles.title: It’s So Hot That Japan Needs a New Word for It
articles.summary: Japan this week recorded its first kokushobi, a term that means “cruel heat day,” as temperatures reached 104 degrees. It is not the only country that has scrambled for a new summer vocabulary.
